title: Mathlib Imports
content: Imports Mathlib tactics, real number basics, finite sets, and inner product spaces. The inner product space structure provides the norm $\|x - y\|$ used in the diameter definition, while finite sets support the partition structure.
mathContext: Requires $\|\cdot\| : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ from inner product spaces, $\text{sSup}$ for the diameter, and $\text{Fin}\,k$ for indexed partitions.

title: Bounded Set in Euclidean Space
content: Defines BoundedSet n as a set of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$, represented as $\text{Fin}\,n \to \mathbb{R}$. This is the domain for Borsuk's partition problem. Note that no boundedness condition is imposed at the type level; diameter finiteness is handled separately.

title: Diameter of a Set
content: The diameter of $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is the supremum of $\|x - y\|$ over all pairs $x, y \in S$. This is the standard metric diameter. The definition uses Lean's $\text{sSup}$ (supremum of a set of reals), which returns $0$ for the empty set — a harmless convention since Borsuk's problem concerns nonempty sets.

title: Small-Diameter Partition
content: IsSmallDiamPartition S k d pieces holds when the $k$ pieces cover $S$, each piece is a subset of $S$, and each piece has diameter strictly less than $d$. This formalizes the decomposition required by Borsuk's conjecture: can every diameter-1 set be partitioned into $\leq n+1$ parts of diameter $< 1$?
mathContext: $S = \bigcup_{i=1}^{k} P_i$ with $P_i \subseteq S$ and $\text{diam}(P_i) < d$ for all $i$

title: Borsuk Number $\alpha(n)$
content: The Borsuk number $\alpha(n)$ is the minimum $k$ such that every diameter-1 set in $\mathbb{R}^n$ can be partitioned into $k$ parts of strictly smaller diameter. It is axiomatized as a function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ since computing it requires solving an extremal geometry problem. Borsuk conjectured $\alpha(n) = n + 1$; this is true for $n \leq 3$ but fails dramatically for $n \geq 64$.

title: Borsuk's Conjecture (1933)
content: States the conjecture as a predicate: borsukConjecture n iff $\alpha(n) \leq n + 1$. This elegant formulation makes it easy to state both positive results ($\alpha(n) \leq n+1$ for small $n$) and counterexamples ($\neg\,\text{borsukConjecture}(n)$ for large $n$) using the same definition.

title: Low-Dimensional Positive Results
content: Axioms asserting Borsuk's conjecture for $n = 2$ (classical, due to Lenz and Hadwiger) and $n = 3$ (Eggleston 1955, also by Grünbaum and Heppes). For $n = 2$, the result follows from the fact that any planar set of diameter 1 can be covered by 3 strips. For $n = 3$, the proof uses the geometry of the Reuleaux triangle and its 3D analogues. The case $n = 1$ is trivial: any interval is already diameter $< 1$ after splitting into 2 parts.

title: Kahn-Kalai Counterexample (1993)
content: Jeff Kahn and Gil Kalai disproved Borsuk's conjecture for $n \geq 2015$ (later improved to $n \geq 2014$). Their construction uses a finite subset of the Boolean cube $\{0,1\}^n$: they select vectors of a specific weight and use the Frankl-Wilson theorem to show that any partition into parts of smaller diameter requires exponentially many parts. Specifically, they showed $\alpha(n) \geq (1.2)^{\sqrt{n}}$, which exceeds $n + 1$ for large $n$. This was one of the most surprising results in discrete geometry, disproving a 60-year-old conjecture.
mathContext: $\forall n \geq 2014,\; \alpha(n) > n + 1$; construction: $A \subseteq \{0,1\}^n$ with $|A| = \binom{n}{n/4}$ and controlled inner products

title: Brouwer-Jenrich Improvement (2014)
content: Andries Brouwer and Thomas Jenrich improved the counterexample dimension threshold from $n \geq 2014$ to $n \geq 64$. Their approach used computer-assisted search over two-distance sets (sets with only two distinct pairwise distances) to find explicit counterexamples in lower dimensions. The gap $4 \leq n \leq 63$ remains the frontier of the problem.

title: Kahn-Kalai Lower Bound on $\alpha(n)$
content: The quantitative lower bound $\alpha(n) \geq (1.2)^{\sqrt{n}}$ for large $n$. This shows the Borsuk number grows at least exponentially in $\sqrt{n}$, spectacularly refuting the linear conjecture $\alpha(n) = n + 1$. The proof uses the Frankl-Wilson theorem applied to layers of the Boolean cube, combined with a graph coloring argument: the partition number equals the chromatic number of the Borsuk graph (vertices = points, edges = diameter pairs).

title: Schramm Upper Bound on $\alpha(n)$
content: Oded Schramm's upper bound $\alpha(n) \leq (\sqrt{3/2} + o(1))^n \approx 1.225^n$ using the illumination body technique and entropy methods. The idea is to illuminate a convex body $K$ with light sources placed at distance $> \text{diam}(K)$; the number of sources needed provides an upper bound on $\alpha(n)$. Combined with the Kahn-Kalai lower bound, this pins down $\alpha(n)$ as being between $\exp(c\sqrt{n})$ and $\exp(Cn)$ — the correct growth rate remains a major open question.

title: Intermediate Dimensions: The Open Frontier
content: For $n = 4$, the Borsuk number satisfies $4 \leq \alpha(4) \leq 5$, but the exact value is unknown. More generally, for $4 \leq n \leq 63$, neither a proof of the conjecture nor a counterexample is known. This range represents the hardest open cases: too small for the algebraic/combinatorial methods of Kahn-Kalai, yet too large for exhaustive geometric arguments. Progress on $n = 4$ would likely require new techniques in computational geometry or polyhedral combinatorics.
